<reason>B won by keeping the motion’s science-per-dollar test live and treating crew advantages as real but concentrated costs to be selected, not a claim on the majority. A’s industrial-base, Hubble/ISS, and “lumpy capability” attacks were the sharper practical case and exploited B’s concession that heavy lift and a Station-class lab would not be guaranteed. A never showed why majority rather than a narrower preserved capability is required, and refused the hypothetical that a same-cost robotic portfolio answering more important questions would change priorities. B’s weighing—that a valuable option can still cost more science than it enables—was the cleaner reason to vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s Rebuttal 2 turn of A’s architecture claim: high fixed costs raise the selection burden instead of entitling crew to most funding, after A declined to cede even if robots answered more important questions at the same cost.</best_rebuttal>
